C1.name: Nokia mobile phones, 2009
C1.who: CEO Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo, 2009, as he might have answered then
C1.answererBelief: We are the global leader with huge scale and margins; the iPhone is a niche high end product and the issue is execution on touch and software, plus a tough recession and aggressive competitors.
C1.expertBelief: Fear that nobody dared say upward. A proud engineering company whose middle managers lied up the chain to protect themselves, and a CEO who could not hear that the platform was dying. Grief and denial dressed as confidence.
C1.recordSays: Symbian too slow to develop for, fragmented software, internal fear and politics, middle management hiding bad news from top, overconfidence and slow decisions (Vuori/Doz, INSEAD study); Elop's 'burning platform' memo 2011.

C2.name: Theranos, 2015
C2.who: Elizabeth Holmes, founder/CEO, autumn 2015 after the WSJ story
C2.answererBelief: We are a visionary company being attacked by an incumbent industry and a hostile press; the technology works and we just need time and to protect our IP.
C2.expertBelief: A story that could not be allowed to be wrong. Secrecy was holding up a lie, and the founder was fused with the narrative; anyone who doubted was pushed out. The real thing is truth being unwelcome.
C2.recordSays: Technology did not work as claimed, results were inaccurate, secrecy and fear culture, board lacked expertise, dissenters fired or threatened with legal action, regulators found lab violations.

C3.name: Twitter, December 2022
C3.who: A surviving engineering manager at Twitter after the acquisition and mass layoffs, December 2022
C3.answererBelief: We lost too many people and nobody knows who owns what; priorities change daily and we are firefighting with half the team.
C3.expertBelief: Fear and loyalty-by-hostage. People stay for visas and paychecks, not belief. Underneath is grief for the colleagues gone, and no trust that decisions are made for reasons.
C3.recordSays: Sudden cuts of about half the staff, loss of institutional knowledge, outages, erratic top-down decisions, an ultimatum to be 'hardcore', unclear ownership, advertisers leaving.

C4.name: Zappos, 2015
C4.who: Tony Hsieh, CEO, 2015 during the holacracy rollout
C4.answererBelief: We need to stay innovative and self-organizing like a city, not a bureaucracy; people just need to adapt and some who resist should take the offer to leave.
C4.expertBelief: A founder in love with an idea who has made it a belief system. Staff are unsettled, losing the clear path of management, and afraid to say the experiment is hurting them. Ideology outrunning the human need for clarity.
C4.recordSays: Around 18 percent of staff left after the buyout offer, confusion over roles and pay and career paths, loss of managers, culture strain; Zappos later moved away from strict holacracy.

C5.name: Family business, unspoken between generations (composite)
C5.who: Daughter, 41, now running a 60-year-old regional building supply company with her father, 74, still in the office every day
C5.answererBelief: Cash flow is tight, margins are shrinking, and we have a hard time hiring good counter staff and drivers.
C5.expertBelief: Dad has never said she is the successor, and she has never asked. Her brother left and it was never discussed. Every decision is secretly a referendum on whether she is allowed to be in charge. Unspoken: permission, and his fear of being unnecessary.

C6.name: Exhausted owner (composite)
C6.who: Owner of a 14-person design and print shop, 52, seventeen years in, answering on a Sunday night
C6.answererBelief: I think the business is just too demanding, or maybe I am burned out, I honestly cannot tell. Customers are fine, money is okay.
C6.expertBelief: The business is fine and she is depleted: she is the bottleneck for every decision, hasn't had a real break in years, and quietly grieves the creative work she used to do. Needs permission to rest and to hand things off, not a new strategy.
